summary: The note surveys rock climbing and bouldering as a growing sport, covering its rising popularity, the difference between roped climbing and bouldering, training, safety advice, community events, and the risks of free soloing. It quotes local gym owners, instructors and experts, and notes safety advances and youth outreach. It closes with an optimistic outlook for the sport's future.
one_line: An overview of rock climbing and bouldering's surge in popularity, covering training, safety, community events, free soloing risks, and youth outreach.
key_facts: Rock climbing and bouldering gained popularity partly through their inclusion in the Tokyo 2020 Olympics.
Emily Nguyen, a local gym owner, said "Since September last year, we've seen a huge increase in interest, especially among younger crowds looking for something beyond traditional sports."
Rock climbing uses harnesses, ropes and protective gear on natural or artificial rock faces, while bouldering is done on small rock formations or artificial walls without ropes or harnesses.
Carlos Garcia, a veteran climber and instructor, said climbing is about understanding your body, using your core, and developing good footwork, not just upper-body strength.
Ascend High, a local climbing gym, runs courses and clinics that start with basic techniques, safety protocols and equipment handling.

Safety expert Alex Brewer says beginners commonly underestimate the physical demands of climbing and overestimate their ability level, and advises starting with qualified instructors in climbing gyms.
The Rocky Heights Climbers Club hosted its annual "Climb Fest" on October 14-15.
Free soloing means climbing without ropes, harnesses or protective gear; debate over it grew after Alex Honnold's free solo ascent of El Capitan in Yosemite National Park.
Sports psychology expert Dr. Lila Robertson said free soloing's margin for error is non-existent and not many have the psychological makeup for it.
Safety advances include improved crash pads for bouldering, more reliable protective gear, and rigorous certification of climbing instructors.
Jake Emerson, who has over a decade of climbing experience, spoke at a climbathon event on November 3, 2023, calling climbing "a lifelong journey".
Outreach programs in schools and youth centers, particularly on International Climbing Day, November 25, introduce children to the sport.
